title: How To Handle Talkative Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Opening with a memory of an interrupting grandfather at Thanksgiving, Linsin argues that unpermitted talking in class is not a minor annoyance but a genuine fairness issue: it wastes instructional time, interrupts other students' learning, and privileges the most outgoing or aggressive voices over the rest of the class. He recounts a conversation with a teacher who tolerated constant talking under the banner of 'open discussion,' and uses her resulting classroom chaos and parent complaints as a cautionary example. His prescribed remedy is straightforward: make hand-raising an enforced classroom rule, apply consequences consistently for calling out or side-talking, and explain to students directly why the rule protects everyone's right to participate. He predicts that, contrary to teacher fears, students respect this enforcement because it reassures them of equal footing in the classroom.
points: Unpermitted talking is not just disruptive but unfair, since it privileges the most outgoing students' voices over everyone else's.
Tolerating constant talk under the banner of 'open discussion' tends to produce chaos and behavior problems rather than richer dialogue.
Hand-raising should be an enforced classroom rule, applied consistently to every instance of calling out or side-talking.
Students generally respect firm enforcement of talking rules because it reassures them of fair, equal access to participate.
quotes: If there are students in your classroom who talk when they’re supposed to be listening or working, academic progress will suffer. Talking without permission wastes time, interrupts the learning of others, and leads to more serious disruptive behavior.
Allowing students to freely talk without permission is like driving an old jalopy; progress only comes in fits and starts, and you’ll never reach top speed.

With 20 to 30 or more students in a classroom, asking students to raise their hands is the only way to ensure fairness. Every student has the right to participate and all should have equal access to the discussion—not just those who are more outgoing, aggressive, or obnoxious.

Too many teachers feel they'll be disliked if they strictly follow such ticky-tacky rules. But the opposite is true. Your students will love you for it because it reassures them that they are equal members of your classroom, free to join in the learning process.
And if you want your classroom to run like a finely tuned Italian sports car, then enforce a consequence every time a student breaks a rule.
